title: Collaborative Document Editor (Session-Based)
description: Design a document editing system where users create, own, share, version, and collaboratively edit documents with access-level controls and session-based editing. Unlike CRDT-based real-time collab (P21), this focuses on **session lifecycle, access control via Strategy Pattern, version history, and sharing**. This is the LLD that shows up at Indian product companies — structured around MVC with clear entity/service/controller separation.
prompt: Design a system where users create, own, share, and collaboratively edit documents with access-level controls (VIEW, COMMENT, EDIT), version history, and session-based editing.
prompt_note: This is the **practical/interview-friendly** version of the collaborative editor problem. No CRDTs or OT — instead, it tests your ability to model: (1) access control as a clean Strategy Pattern, (2) session lifecycle (open → edit → save → close), (3) version vs snapshot distinction, (4) sharing with granular permissions. Indian product companies (Flipkart, Swiggy, PhonePe, Atlassian) ask this exact variant.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "What access levels are supported when sharing a document?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Three levels: VIEW (read-only), COMMENT (view + add comments), EDIT (full editing). The owner has all privileges plus delete and share."
clarifying_questions.why: Four distinct permission tiers → **Strategy Pattern** with one policy class per level. Adding a new level (e.g., SUGGEST) = one new class.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "How does editing work — direct mutation or within a session?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "All edits must occur within an editor session. User opens a session → edits (auto-snapshot) → explicitly saves (creates a version) → closes session."
clarifying_questions.why: **EditSession is a first-class entity** with lifecycle (ACTIVE/CLOSED), its own Snapshot, and access validation. This is NOT just 'call updateContent()' — there's a whole state machine.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "What's the difference between a snapshot and a version?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Snapshot = ephemeral, auto-saved within a session, overwritten on each edit. Version = immutable, explicitly created on 'save', permanent in version history."
clarifying_questions.why: Critical distinction. Snapshot has `sessionId + updatedAt` (mutable, ephemeral). Version has `versionNumber + savedBy + message` (immutable, permanent). The *fields tell the story*.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Can multiple users have active edit sessions on the same document?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes — each user gets their own session with their own snapshot. On save, use optimistic locking (check version number hasn't changed). If conflict → user must refresh."
clarifying_questions.why: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking — a concurrency stance the interviewer expects. Mention both, let them choose.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Can comments exist as a separate feature, not just inline edits?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes — comments are positioned (start, end) on the document text. Users with COMMENT access can add them but not edit the document."
clarifying_questions.why: If you don't model Comment as an entity, the COMMENT access level is meaningless — what does it *do*?

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Revert to a previous version — does it create a new version or overwrite?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Append-only history. Reverting to version 3 creates a NEW version (v6) with v3's content. No destructive rewrite."
clarifying_questions.why: Immutable version history = audit trail. Same principle as event sourcing.

core: **Document CRUD:** users create and own documents. Only owner can delete.
**Share with access levels:** share documents with VIEW, COMMENT, or EDIT access. Only owner can share/revoke.
**Session-based editing:** all edits occur within an EditSession (open → edit → save → close).
**Auto-snapshot:** each edit within a session overwrites an ephemeral Snapshot (not a version).
**Explicit save → immutable Version:** user explicitly saves, creating a permanent Version with version number and message.
**Revert:** revert to any previous version (creates a NEW version — append-only history).
**Comments:** users with COMMENT+ access can add positioned comments. Author or owner can resolve them.
**Revoke sharing / delete documents:** owner can revoke shares, delete cascades (closes sessions, removes shares).
out_of_scope: Real-time collaborative editing (CRDT/OT), rich text formatting, persistence/DB, authentication (assume JWT → userId).

core: **SOLID throughout:** Strategy Pattern for access control, Factory for policy creation, Observer for notifications.
**Access enforcement at the service layer** — not the caller's responsibility. Every service method resolves access before proceeding.
**Thread-safety on concurrent edit sessions** — optimistic locking on save (check versionNum hasn't changed).
**No partial saves, no orphaned snapshots** — consistent data at all times.
out_of_scope: Distributed deployment, caching, full-text search, pagination.

primary_scope: Document lifecycle: create → share → open session → edit → save → revert → delete
Access control: owner=all privileges, EDIT=edit+comment+view, COMMENT=comment+view, VIEW=view only
Session lifecycle: ACTIVE → edits update Snapshot → explicit save creates Version → CLOSED
Version history: append-only, revert creates a new version with old content
Comment lifecycle: add (COMMENT+ access) → resolve (author or owner)
termination_points: `SessionNotFoundException` / `SessionNotActiveException` — bad session ID or editing a CLOSED session
`VersionNotFoundException` — requested versionNumber doesn't exist in history
`ConflictException` — optimistic locking: versionNum changed since session opened
entity_intro: This problem has **rich entity behavior** — Document has `applyEdit()`, `revertTo()`, `isOwnedBy()` instead of just getters/setters. This kills the 'anemic domain model' critique that interviewers look for. EditSession is a **first-class entity** with state, lifecycle methods, and Snapshot ownership — not a disconnected box.

entities.name: User
entities.role: **Model.** id, name, email, createdAt. Identity entity — referenced by Document (owner), Share (sharedBy/sharedWith), EditSession, Comment (author).

entities.name: Document
entities.role: **Model with behavior.** id, name, content (current), owner, currentVersionNum, `List<Version>` versionHistory. **Methods:** `applyEdit(newContent)`, `incrementVersion()`, `revertTo(version)`, `isOwnedBy(user)`. NOT anemic — encapsulates domain logic.

entities.name: Version
entities.role: **Model (immutable).** id, versionNumber, documentId, content, savedBy (User), message, createdAt. **No setters** — once created, a version never changes. This is the permanent audit trail.

entities.name: Snapshot
entities.role: **Model (ephemeral).** id, sessionId, documentId, content, updatedAt. One per active session — overwritten on each edit. Discarded when session closes. **Key distinction from Version:** mutable, temporary, tied to a session.

entities.name: EditSession
entities.role: **Model + state machine.** id, documentId, user, accessLevel, state (ACTIVE/CLOSED), currentSnapshot, openedAt, closedAt. **Methods:** `isActive()`, `close()`, `canEdit()`, `canComment()`. The session owns the Snapshot and enforces access within its scope.

entities.name: Share
entities.role: **Model.** id, documentId, sharedBy (User), sharedWith (User), accessLevel (ENUM), sharedOn. The link between a Document and a non-owner User's permissions.

entities.name: Comment
entities.role: **Model.** id, documentId, author (User), content, positionStart, positionEnd, resolved (boolean), createdAt. Positioned on document text. **Methods:** `resolve()`. Without this entity, COMMENT access level would be meaningless.

entities.name: AccessPolicy (Strategy interface)
entities.role: **Strategy Pattern interface.** `canView()`, `canComment()`, `canEdit()`, `canDelete()`, `canShare()`. Four implementations: **ViewPolicy** (view only), **CommentPolicy** (view + comment), **EditPolicy** (view + comment + edit), **OwnerPolicy** (all). Eliminates if-else chains in every service method.

entities.name: AccessPolicyFactory
entities.role: **Factory.** Maps `AccessLevel` enum → concrete `AccessPolicy` implementation. Single responsibility. `getPolicy(AccessLevel.EDIT) → new EditPolicy()`.

relationships.rel: N→1 Document, N→1 User (sharedBy), N→1 User (sharedWith)

relationships.owns: documentId, author, content, position range, resolved flag

mvc_note: **Full MVC separation.** **Model** = User, Document, Version, Snapshot, EditSession, Share, Comment, AccessLevel/SessionState enums. **Service** = DocumentService (CRUD + versioning), SessionService (session lifecycle + editing), ShareService (sharing + access resolution), CommentService (comment CRUD), AccessPolicy implementations. **Controller** = DocumentController, SessionController, ShareController, CommentController — each delegates to its service. **Access checks happen in services, not controllers.**

methods.name: (each implements AccessPolicy with different true/false combos)

schema_note: **Unique constraint** on `shares(document_id, shared_with_user_id)` prevents duplicate shares. **Index** on `(document_id, version_number)` for fast version lookup. Snapshots are ephemeral — in production, these could be in Redis rather than SQL. Sessions with `state=ACTIVE` are indexed for 'find active sessions for this document' queries.

code_sections.label: Enums + AccessPolicy Strategy Pattern
code_sections.flow: **AccessLevel** enum → fed to **AccessPolicyFactory** → returns the correct **AccessPolicy** implementation. Every service method calls `ShareService.resolveAccess(user, doc)` → gets an AccessPolicy → checks `policy.canEdit()` or `policy.canComment()` before proceeding. **No if-else chains** in service code — OCP enforced.

code_sections.label: Model — Document (rich, not anemic) + Version + Snapshot + EditSession
code_sections.flow: **Document** has real behavior: `applyEdit()` updates content + timestamp. `revertTo(v)` copies version content. `incrementVersion()` returns next versionNum. **Version** is immutable — no setters, final fields, created once. **Snapshot** is mutable — overwritten on each edit within a session. **EditSession** has state machine: ACTIVE → CLOSED.

code_sections.label: Service — ShareService (access resolution is the core)
code_sections.flow: **`resolveAccess(user, document)`** is the single most important method. Every other service calls it before doing anything. Logic: if user is owner → `OwnerPolicy`. Else: find Share for this user+document → `AccessPolicyFactory.getPolicy(share.accessLevel)`. No share found → throw `UserNotHaveAccessException`.
code_sections.edge_cases: Sharing with yourself → reject. Sharing when you're not the owner → reject. Duplicate share → `UserAlreadyHasAccessException`. Revoke → also closes any active sessions the target has.

code_sections.label: Service — SessionService (session lifecycle + editing)
code_sections.flow: **`openSession()`:** resolveAccess → create EditSession → create initial Snapshot from document's current content. **`editDocument()`:** validate session ACTIVE + canEdit() → overwrite snapshot content → return snapshot. **`closeSession()`:** set state=CLOSED, discard snapshot. Each edit within a session just updates the ephemeral snapshot — **not the document**. Only `saveDocument` (in DocumentService) commits snapshot content to the document.
code_sections.edge_cases: Opening a session with VIEW access → allowed (user can view, just can't edit). Editing with VIEW/COMMENT → throw `DocumentNotEditableException`. Editing a CLOSED session → throw `SessionNotActiveException`. Session owner mismatch → throw.

code_sections.label: Service — DocumentService (CRUD + versioning + save)
code_sections.flow: **`createDocument()`:** create Document → create initial Version (v1) → store. **`saveDocument(sessionId)`:** get session → get snapshot content → create new Version → increment versionNum → apply edit to document → return Version. **`revertToVersion()`:** find version → `document.revertTo(v)` → create NEW version capturing the revert → append-only history. **`deleteDocument()`:** owner only → close all sessions → remove all shares → remove document.
code_sections.edge_cases: Save on a CLOSED session → throw. Save when version has changed (optimistic locking) → throw `ConflictException`. Revert to non-existent version → throw. Delete by non-owner → throw.

patterns.name: Strategy Pattern → AccessPolicy
patterns.why: **The single biggest design win.** Four access levels, each defining a different set of permissions. Instead of `if (level == EDIT) { ... } else if (level == COMMENT) { ... }` scattered through every service method, we encapsulate each level's permissions in one class. Services call `policy.canEdit()` — they don't know or care which policy is behind it. **Adding SUGGEST access level = one new class, zero changes to services.** This is OCP in action.

patterns.name: Factory Pattern → AccessPolicyFactory
patterns.why: Maps `AccessLevel` enum to the correct `AccessPolicy` implementation. Single responsibility — the factory knows how to construct policies; the services know how to use them. If policy construction becomes complex (e.g., requires config), the factory handles it.

patterns.name: Memento Pattern (implicit) → Version History
patterns.why: Each Version is an immutable snapshot of the document at a point in time. The version history is an **append-only log of mementos**. Revert doesn't destroy history — it creates a new memento from an old one. This is the Memento Pattern applied to document versioning. Same principle as Git commits.

patterns.name: Observer Pattern (extension)
patterns.why: When a document is shared, the target user should be notified. When someone comments, the document owner should be notified. When a version is saved, active viewers might want to refresh. These are all natural Observer events — decouple with a listener/event bus. Not implemented but mentioned as extension.

concurrency.issue: Two EDIT users open sessions and save concurrently — last-write-wins data loss
concurrency.fix: **Optimistic locking.** When a session opens, record the document's `currentVersionNum`. On save, check: 'is the document's current version still what I saw at session open?' If yes → save succeeds, version increments. If no → `ConflictException` — user must refresh their session, see the new version, merge manually, and retry. **Alternative: pessimistic locking** — only one EDIT session active per document. Simpler but less concurrent.

concurrency.issue: Edit and delete race — user editing while owner deletes the document
concurrency.fix: `deleteDocument()` calls `sessionService.closeAllSessionsForDocument()` first — all active sessions are closed. The next edit attempt by the editing user hits `SessionNotActiveException`. The document is then removed from the store.

concurrency.issue: Revoke share while user has active session
concurrency.fix: `revokeShare()` should also close any active sessions the revoked user has. After revoke, their next action will fail with `UserNotHaveAccessException` (no share exists anymore).

concurrency.issue: Concurrent snapshot updates within a session
concurrency.fix: Each session is used by one user. Concurrent edits within a single session aren't expected (one user, one browser tab). If they were (e.g., multiple tabs), `Snapshot.updateContent()` could be `synchronized`.

deep_dives.question: Why is AccessPolicy a Strategy Pattern and not just an if-else on the enum?
deep_dives.answer: **Open/Closed Principle.** With if-else: adding SUGGEST access level means finding and modifying every service method that checks access. With Strategy: add `SuggestPolicy implements AccessPolicy` — one new class, zero changes to existing code. **Also:** policies can have complex logic (e.g., 'EditPolicy can edit only during business hours'). A class encapsulates that; an if-else can't.

deep_dives.question: Why is Snapshot separate from Version? Can't you just use Versions for everything?
deep_dives.answer: **Different lifecycles.** Snapshot is **mutable + ephemeral** — overwritten on every keystroke, discarded on session close. Version is **immutable + permanent** — created only on explicit save, never modified, kept forever for audit. If every keystroke created a Version, the version history would have 10,000 entries for a 10-paragraph document. Snapshot absorbs the noise; Version captures the signal.

deep_dives.question: Why is EditSession a first-class entity and not just a method parameter?
deep_dives.answer: **Sessions have state and lifecycle.** An EditSession tracks: which user, which document, what access level, is it active, what's the current snapshot, when was it opened. This is too much state for a method parameter. Making it an entity lets us: (1) validate state on every edit call, (2) close all sessions on document delete, (3) prevent edits on closed sessions, (4) associate snapshots with sessions for cleanup.

deep_dives.question: How does revert work without destroying history?
deep_dives.answer: **Append-only.** Reverting to version 3 from version 5 creates version 6 with version 3's content. History: v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6(reverted from v3). No destructive rewrite. This means: (1) audit trail is intact — you can see WHO reverted WHEN, (2) you can undo the revert by reverting to v5, (3) concurrent users don't lose their reference to v4/v5. **Same principle as Git** — revert is a new commit, not a force-push.

deep_dives.question: Why enforce access at the service layer, not the controller?
deep_dives.answer: **Single enforcement point.** Controllers can be bypassed (internal calls, different endpoints, batch jobs). If access checks live in the service, **every code path** goes through them. The controller is just a thin HTTP adapter — it parses requests and delegates. The service is the authority. This is a fundamental **separation of concerns** that interviewers look for.

deep_dives.question: What if the Comment entity didn't exist — what would COMMENT access level even mean?
deep_dives.answer: **Nothing.** If you model COMMENT as an access level but don't model Comment as an entity, you've created a permission that permits... nothing observable. The interviewer will ask 'what can a COMMENT user do?' and you'll have no answer. **Entities and permissions must be aligned.** Every permission must map to at least one entity operation. This is why modeling Comment was essential even though the prompt didn't explicitly describe it.

deep_dives.question: How would you implement real-time collaboration on top of this design?
deep_dives.answer: **Two paths.** (1) **Add CRDT/OT layer (P21):** replace the Snapshot text with a CRDT document. Each edit generates an Operation that's broadcast via WebSocket. The session-based model still works — sessions open/close, but the edit flow goes through the CRDT. (2) **Keep it simple:** use the existing session+snapshot model with a shared document lock and a 'refresh' mechanism. User A saves → User B's session detects the version change → B refreshes. Not real-time, but practical for many use cases (like Google Docs before 2010).

deep_dives.question: How would you add an audit log?
deep_dives.answer: **Observer Pattern.** Fire events for every state-changing operation: `DocumentCreated`, `DocumentShared`, `SessionOpened`, `DocumentEdited`, `VersionSaved`, `DocumentReverted`, `ShareRevoked`. An `AuditListener` subscribes and writes each event to an append-only log with: who, what, when, documentId. The services fire events; the audit system consumes them. **Fully decoupled** — adding audit doesn't change any service code.
